Strengthen engagement planning by incorporating stakeholder input and risk assessment to better align audit objectives and procedures with the organization's most significant risks.
Increase documentation requirements to improve audit quality.
Reduce discussions with management to preserve auditor independence.
e: An effective engagement starts with a solid risk assessment, so the way to increase future value here is strengthening engagement planning by incorporating stakeholder input and risk assessment to better align audit objectives and procedures with the organization's most significant risks. Documentation quality doesn't address whether the right risks were even selected for audit, communicating with management doesn't impair independence when handled appropriately, and testing every process regardless of risk is inefficient and contrary to a risk-based approach.

q: The CAE notices that management's quarterly risk reports consistently describe major initiatives as "low risk," despite frequent project delays, cost overruns, and missed objectives. Interviews reveal that business unit leaders believe reporting higher risks will negatively affect their performance evaluations. Which conclusion is most appropriate?
c: Risk reporting should remain unchanged because project performance is measured separately.
Internal audit should recommend increasing project budgets to reduce future overruns.
The organization may exhibit a weak risk culture in which performance incentives discourage transparent risk reporting, reducing the effectiveness of governance and enterprise risk management.
Management should classify every strategic initiative as high risk to improve reporting accuracy.
e: A weak risk culture in which performance incentives discourage transparent risk reporting, where business unit leaders downplay risk to protect their performance evaluations, undermines effective governance and enterprise risk management, so internal audit should evaluate whether current incentives are encouraging transparent communication. Leaving reporting unchanged ignores that project performance and risk reporting are closely linked, increasing project budgets doesn't touch the underlying cultural issue, and forcing every initiative into a high-risk classification would just as artificially distort the reporting.

q: Internal audit develops a dashboard that continuously monitors duplicate vendor payments. Several business units begin using the dashboard to monitor their own controls and request that internal audit maintain it permanently. What is the most appropriate response?
c: Continue operating the dashboard because internal audit originally developed it.
Assume ownership of the monitoring process because it improves organizational efficiency.
Discontinue the dashboard immediately because management should never use internal audit-developed tools.
Transfer responsibility for operating the dashboard to management while internal audit may continue to evaluate its effectiveness.
e: Operating a management control, even one internal audit built, is a management responsibility, so the dashboard should be handed over to management to run, with internal audit free to keep evaluating its effectiveness rather than operating it. Continuing to run it could impair objectivity if internal audit later audits the very process the dashboard monitors, organizational efficiency doesn't justify internal audit taking on a management role, and there's nothing wrong with management using a tool internal audit developed as long as management owns it going forward.

q: A severe earthquake disrupts one of the organization's major distribution centers. Although the business continuity plan was activated successfully, auditors discover that several key suppliers had never been included in recovery planning. What is the most appropriate conclusion?
c: The recovery plan should be evaluated for gaps in third-party dependency planning despite the successful activation.
The recovery plan was effective because business operations eventually resumed.
Recovery planning should focus only on facilities directly owned by the organization.
Supplier disruptions are outside the scope of business continuity planning.
e: A successful activation of the business continuity plan doesn't mean the plan is comprehensive, so the omission of critical suppliers from business continuity planning indicates a weakness in third-party dependency management and organizational resilience, even though recovery was ultimately successful. Recovering operations doesn't by itself prove the planning was thorough, supplier disruptions are a legitimate part of continuity planning rather than outside its scope, and continuity planning needs to extend beyond facilities the organization directly owns.

q: The audit committee receives lengthy audit reports containing extensive technical detail but very little analysis of strategic implications or emerging risks. Several committee members express difficulty identifying the issues requiring their attention. Which improvement would most enhance board oversight?
c: Increase the level of technical detail included in every report.
Present concise reports emphasizing significant risks, root causes, trends, and matters requiring board attention.
Eliminate management responses to reduce report length.
Replace written reports with verbal presentations during committee meetings.
e: The board benefits from concise, risk-focused reporting that surfaces significant risks, root causes, trends, and matters needing its attention, rather than dense technical detail, so that's the improvement most likely to help. Adding even more technical detail would further obscure the issues that matter, cutting management's responses out would remove useful context, and moving to verbal-only presentations would lose the documentation value that written reports provide.

q: The internal audit function has consistently exceeded every operational performance target established by the CAE. Nevertheless, an external assessment concludes that internal audit provides limited strategic insight and is viewed primarily as a compliance function. Which action would most improve the internal audit function's long-term effectiveness?
c: Reduce consulting activities to focus exclusively on assurance engagements.
Increase the number of compliance engagements completed each year.
Expand engagement planning to include emerging risks, strategic objectives, and forward-looking analyses that support board decision-making.
Increase individual auditor productivity targets to improve overall efficiency.
e: Modern internal auditing is expected to deliver insight and foresight alongside assurance, so expanding engagement planning to cover emerging risks, strategic objectives, and forward-looking analysis is what would shift the function's perceived value and improve long-term effectiveness. Doing more compliance work would only reinforce the compliance-only perception, cutting consulting activity ignores that well-managed consulting work can add organizational value, and pushing productivity targets higher improves efficiency without touching strategic relevance.

q: The organization has separate compliance, quality assurance, information security, and risk management functions. During audit planning, the CAE notices that all four functions intend to review the same procurement process within the next six months. What should the CAE do?
c: Request management to determine which assurance provider should perform the review.
Cancel the internal audit engagement because sufficient assurance will already be provided.
Perform the engagement independently because internal audit should never rely on the work of other assurance providers.

Coordinate with other assurance providers within the organization's combined assurance approach to evaluate opportunities for reliance, eliminate unnecessary duplication, and maintain appropriate assurance coverage.
e: The CAE should coordinate with other assurance providers within the organization's combined assurance approach to look for opportunities to rely on their work and eliminate unnecessary duplication while still making sure risk coverage stays appropriate. Other functions planning to look at the same process doesn't automatically remove the need for internal audit's own involvement, appropriately relying on other providers' work after evaluating its quality is different from never relying on it at all, and it's the CAE, not management, who remains responsible for determining internal audit's coverage.

q: Management proposes closing several regional offices to reduce operating costs. The financial analysis supports the proposal, but little consideration has been given to customer experience or operational resilience. What should internal audit evaluate?
c: Whether management considered relevant strategic risks, assumptions, and potential unintended consequences before making the decision.
Whether the projected financial savings are sufficient to justify the decision regardless of any potential operational or customer-related impacts.
Whether management selected the best strategic alternative available rather than considering other possible courses of action.
Whether the board should approve or reject the proposal based on the expected financial and operational outcomes.
e: Internal audit evaluates the quality of management's governance and decision-making process rather than the business decision itself, so the focus here should be on whether management considered the relevant strategic risks, assumptions, and potential unintended consequences of closing the offices. Whether the projected savings justify the move is a management call, internal audit doesn't decide whether the board should reject the proposal, and regional managers' support doesn't tell you whether the underlying decision-making process was sound.

q: Following several engagements, the CAE notices that different audit teams repeatedly identify similar root causes involving inadequate management supervision. Which action is most appropriate?
c: Require every engagement to include identical recommendations to improve consistency.
Analyze recurring observations across engagements and communicate systemic issues to senior management and the board.
Eliminate root cause analysis because management is responsible for corrective actions.
Report each engagement independently without identifying organizational trends.
e: Spotting the same root cause — inadequate management supervision — showing up across multiple engagements is exactly the kind of systemic pattern internal audit should analyze and escalate to senior management and the board, rather than treating each engagement in isolation. Reporting engagements independently without flagging the trend risks hiding a broader organizational issue, dropping root cause analysis would undercut the value of audit recommendations, and forcing identical recommendations across engagements ignores that each one has its own specific circumstances.

q: An engagement reveals that employees are using publicly available generative AI tools to prepare customer communications. No organizational policy governs acceptable use, data protection, or approval requirements. Which observation is most significant?
c: Employees should discontinue all use of AI technologies.
The issue should be addressed only by the information technology department.

The absence of AI governance—including policies governing acceptable use, data protection, human oversight, and accountability—may expose the organization to operational, legal, regulatory, ethical, and information security risks.
Public AI tools present minimal risk because they are widely available.
e: Employees using public generative AI tools with no policy on acceptable use, data protection, human oversight, or accountability is a governance gap that can expose the organization to operational, legal, regulatory, ethical, and information security risk, so that absence of AI governance is the most significant observation. The issue is the missing oversight, not the technology itself, so telling employees to stop using AI misses the point, wide availability of these tools doesn't make them risk-free, and AI governance needs legal, compliance, and business stakeholders involved, not just IT.

q: The audit committee asks the CAE how internal audit measures its success. The CAE currently reports audit plan completion, budget performance, and report issuance timeliness. Which additional measure would provide the greatest insight into the internal audit function's effectiveness?
c: Percentage of audit recommendations accepted by management.
Average number of workpapers completed per engagement.
Average number of findings reported during each engagement.
Evidence that internal audit activities contributed to stronger governance, improved risk management, or more effective controls.
e: The strongest measure of internal audit's effectiveness is evidence that its work actually strengthened governance, risk management, or controls, which goes beyond the operational metrics the CAE is already reporting. Workpaper volume just measures activity, management accepting recommendations is a useful but incomplete signal since acceptance doesn't guarantee organizational improvement, and the number of findings says nothing about how significant or impactful the audit work actually was.

q: The organization recently launched a digital subscription business that now generates 15% of total revenue. The activity is not yet included in the audit universe because it was created after the last annual planning cycle. What should the CAE do?
c: Update the audit universe to reflect the new activity, assess its relative risk, and determine whether revisions to the current audit plan are warranted.
Exclude the activity until it generates at least 25% of organizational revenue.
Wait until the next annual risk assessment before adding the activity to the audit universe.
Audit the activity immediately because all new business initiatives represent high risk.
e: The audit universe should stay current with organizational change, so a new business line generating 15% of revenue should be added to the audit universe, its risk assessed, and any warranted revisions made to the current audit plan rather than left out until the next full cycle. Waiting for the next annual risk assessment could delay assurance over a genuinely significant new area, assuming every new initiative is automatically high risk skips the structured risk assessment that should decide that, and revenue thresholds alone shouldn't determine whether something belongs in the audit universe.

q: During an engagement, auditors learn that several managers routinely bypass procurement policies by dividing purchases into smaller transactions that fall below approval thresholds. Management argues that the practice improves operational efficiency and has not resulted in financial loss. What is the most appropriate conclusion?
c: The issue should be reported only if the total purchases exceed the organization's materiality threshold.
The practice represents a governance concern because it intentionally circumvents established controls regardless of financial impact.
The practice is acceptable because management is responsible for operational efficiency.
No finding should be reported because no fraud or financial loss has occurred.
e: Deliberately splitting purchases to dodge approval thresholds circumvents an approved control and weakens governance and accountability regardless of whether any financial loss has actually occurred, so this is a governance concern that should be reported as such. Operational efficiency doesn't justify bypassing an approved control, the absence of fraud or loss doesn't mean there's nothing to report since control deficiencies are evaluated on risk rather than actual outcomes, and governance concerns like this aren't determined by whether a materiality threshold has been crossed.

q: While planning an audit of inventory management, the engagement team identifies two major risks that were not included in the preliminary scope because they emerged after planning began. What is the most appropriate action?
c: Document the risks for consideration during the next audit cycle.
Continue with the approved scope to avoid delaying the engagement.
Modify the engagement objectives and procedures as appropriate after evaluating the significance of the newly identified risks.
Expand testing only if management formally requests additional audit work.
e: Engagement planning is an iterative process, so when significant new risks surface after planning has started, the team should evaluate their significance and modify the engagement objectives and procedures as appropriate. Sticking rigidly to the original scope risks reducing the engagement's effectiveness, deferring the risks to next cycle could expose the organization unnecessarily in the meantime, and while management's input is valuable, it's internal audit that determines the engagement's scope.

q: During a quarterly meeting, the audit committee asks the CAE to begin reporting on emerging ESG and cybersecurity risks in addition to financial reporting risks. Senior management believes those topics should remain within management reporting. What should the CAE do?
c: Limit reporting to financial risks because they are the board's primary responsibility.
Report only risks specifically requested by senior management.
Incorporate information that enables the board to fulfill its oversight responsibilities.
Delay reporting until an engagement covering those areas has been completed.
e: The CAE should provide information that helps the board exercise effective oversight, including significant nonfinancial risks such as emerging ESG and cybersecurity exposures, rather than restricting reporting to only financial matters or only what management wants shared. Reference: Standard 8.1 - Board Interaction.

q: A newly approved audit requires expertise in artificial intelligence that no member of the internal audit activity possesses. The audit is considered high priority. What is the BEST course of action?
c: Remove the engagement from the audit plan.
Assign the engagement to the most experienced auditor available.
Obtain the necessary expertise through appropriate resources.
Reduce the audit scope to match existing competencies.
e: The CAE should ensure sufficient competencies are available to complete the engagement effectively, which may mean bringing in outside expertise rather than dropping the engagement, assigning it to someone without the needed skill set, or shrinking the scope to fit existing gaps. Reference: Standard 8.2 - Resources.

q: Senior management decides not to implement a recommendation addressing a significant governance weakness. The CAE believes the residual risk exceeds the board's risk tolerance. What should the CAE do?
c: Remove the recommendation from the final report.
Accept management's decision because risk ownership belongs to management.
Communicate the matter through the established escalation process.
Perform another audit before notifying the board.
e: When a significant issue exceeds the organization's established risk tolerance, it should be escalated according to the agreed-upon board communication process rather than silently accepted, buried, or delayed behind another engagement. Reference: Standard 8.1 - Board Interaction.

q: The organization changes its strategic direction by entering several new international markets. The approved annual audit plan has not yet begun. What should the CAE do FIRST?
c: Continue the existing plan because it has board approval.
Revise the audit plan to reflect the changed risk environment.
Perform only advisory engagements during the transition.
Wait until next year's planning cycle.
e: The audit plan should remain aligned with the organization's current strategies and risks, so a major strategic shift like entering new international markets calls for revising the plan rather than sticking rigidly to an outdated one or waiting a full year.

q: An external quality assessment identified several improvement opportunities but concluded the internal audit activity generally conforms to the Standards. Which action is MOST appropriate?
c: Report only the positive conclusion.
Ignore recommendations because conformance was achieved.
Develop improvement actions and communicate appropriate results.
Schedule another external assessment immediately.
e: Quality assessment results, including improvement opportunities identified alongside a generally-conforms conclusion, should be used to strengthen the internal audit activity through continuous improvement and appropriate communication of results, not simply reported selectively or set aside. Reference: Quality Assurance Standards.

q: While planning an audit of an automated purchasing system, auditors discover that over 95% of transactions are processed without manual intervention. Which audit approach is MOST appropriate?
c: Increase manual sampling only.
Focus primarily on application controls and automated processes.
Ignore automated controls because no manual review exists.
Test only transactions exceeding a monetary threshold.
e: Highly automated environments require greater emphasis on application and automated controls, since that's where the vast majority of processing risk actually resides, rather than relying on manual sampling or a simple dollar threshold.

q: A senior internal auditor consistently produces high-quality work but has limited knowledge of cloud computing, an area that will dominate next year's audit plan. Which action BEST supports the internal audit activity?
c: Exclude cloud audits from the plan.
Assign another employee permanently.
Invest in developing the required competency.
Delay technology audits indefinitely.
e: Internal audit competencies should evolve with the organization's changing risks, so investing in developing the auditor's cloud computing knowledge better supports the function than dropping the coverage area or indefinitely delaying it.

q: An engagement identified numerous minor findings but only one issue that could materially affect achievement of organizational objectives. How should the CAE communicate the results?
c: Give equal emphasis to every finding.
Highlight the significant issue while presenting supporting observations appropriately.
Report only the material issue.
Allow management to determine report emphasis.
e: Communications should clearly emphasize the matters most important to stakeholders, meaning the material issue should stand out while the minor findings are still presented appropriately rather than given equal weight or omitted entirely.

q: Management has implemented controls that reduce operational risk but significantly increase compliance risk. What should internal audit evaluate FIRST?
c: Whether total residual risk remains acceptable.
Whether operating costs have increased.
Whether management documented every control.
Whether employees support the new process.
e: Internal audit evaluates whether risk responses appropriately manage overall residual risk, so when a control trade-off shifts risk from one category to another, the priority is assessing whether the combined residual risk is still acceptable, not cost, documentation, or employee sentiment alone.

q: The CAE reports that 100% of the annual audit plan was completed. However, the board remains dissatisfied because major emerging risks were not addressed. Which performance measure would BEST complement plan completion?
c: Number of audit reports issued.
Average report length.
Coverage of significant organizational risks.
Percentage of scheduled audit hours used.
e: Performance should measure whether internal audit addressed the organization's most significant risks, not merely completed planned work, so tracking coverage of significant risks better reflects value than activity counts like reports issued or hours used.

q: Following several acquisitions, the board asks internal audit to determine whether governance practices are operating consistently across all subsidiaries. Management proposes limiting the engagement to reviewing only documented policies because visiting every location would be costly. Which approach is BEST?
c: Accept management's proposal because governance begins with documented policies.
Evaluate whether governance processes are operating effectively, using procedures sufficient to support a conclusion.
Review only subsidiaries with prior audit findings.
Limit testing to financial reporting controls because governance is management's responsibility.
e: Governance assurance requires evaluating how governance actually operates in practice, not merely whether policies exist on paper, so the engagement should use procedures sufficient to support a conclusion rather than being scoped down to a document review or narrowed to only flagged subsidiaries.

q: During planning, management rates a newly implemented cloud platform as low risk because no security incidents have occurred. However, internal audit identifies several critical control weaknesses. What should the audit team do?
c: Accept management's risk assessment because management owns risk.
Base audit procedures solely on historical incidents.
Independently assess the risk when determining engagement priorities.
Delay the engagement until sufficient incident data exists.
e: Internal audit uses independent professional judgment when assessing risk, so identified control weaknesses should inform the audit team's own risk assessment rather than simply deferring to management's incident-free rating or waiting for more historical data to accumulate.

q: While performing an engagement, auditors obtain evidence supporting two different conclusions regarding the effectiveness of a key control. What is the BEST action?
c: Report the more favorable conclusion to maintain objectivity.
Expand procedures until sufficient appropriate evidence supports a conclusion.
Average the results and conclude the control is partially effective.
Ask management which conclusion is most reasonable.
e: Conclusions should be supported by sufficient and appropriate evidence, so conflicting evidence calls for expanding procedures until a well-supported conclusion can be reached, rather than picking the favorable result, averaging the findings, or deferring the judgment call to management.

q: Internal audit uses data analytics to identify unusual journal entries. The analysis identifies hundreds of anomalies, but most are legitimate business transactions. What should the auditors do NEXT?
c: Report every anomaly as a control deficiency.
Ignore the results because the analytics produced false positives.
Perform additional procedures to determine which anomalies represent audit issues.
Conclude automated controls are ineffective.
e: Analytical results require validation before conclusions are reached, so the next step is performing additional procedures to separate genuine audit issues from legitimate transactions, rather than treating every anomaly as a deficiency or dismissing the analysis outright.

q: During an audit committee meeting, directors ask the CAE whether a recently discovered operational issue should immediately be classified as a significant risk requiring board attention. The available evidence is incomplete. What is the BEST response?
c: Escalate immediately because all unresolved issues should be reported.
Delay discussion until the next quarterly meeting.
Explain the current facts, the remaining uncertainties, and the planned assessment.
Wait until management determines the significance.
e: Board communication should be timely, balanced, and based on available evidence, so the best response lays out what is currently known, what remains uncertain, and how the matter will be further assessed, rather than over-escalating an incomplete picture or delaying the conversation entirely. Reference: Standard 8.1 - Board Interaction.

q: The audit plan requires 8,000 hours. Available staff can provide only 6,500 hours. Management refuses additional funding but expects the original plan to be completed. What should the CAE do?
c: Require auditors to work additional unpaid hours.
Complete every engagement with reduced testing.
Inform the board of the resource shortfall and its impact.
Eliminate documentation requirements to improve efficiency.
e: Resource limitations affecting the audit plan should be communicated to the board so it can make an informed decision, rather than being absorbed through unpaid overtime, quietly thinning testing across every engagement, or cutting documentation. Reference: Standard 8.2 - Resources.

q: The CAE wants to evaluate whether internal audit is creating value rather than simply completing engagements. Which metric BEST supports this objective?
c: Average audit report length.
Percentage of recommendations that reduced significant risks.
Number of meetings attended by auditors.
Average fieldwork hours per engagement.
e: Value is better reflected by measuring improvements to significant organizational risks, such as the percentage of recommendations that actually reduced those risks, than by activity-based measures like report length, meeting attendance, or hours logged.

q: An audit identifies control weaknesses that individually appear immaterial. Collectively, however, they expose the organization to substantial financial loss. What should internal audit conclude?
c: Report each issue separately as immaterial.
Evaluate the combined effect before reaching a conclusion.
Disregard the issues because no individual weakness is significant.
Recommend increasing insurance coverage instead.
e: Audit conclusions should consider the cumulative effect of related deficiencies, so the team needs to evaluate the combined exposure rather than assessing each weakness in isolation, dismissing them individually, or substituting a conclusion with an unrelated recommendation like more insurance.

q: A business unit consistently implements audit recommendations promptly but rarely consults internal audit during major organizational changes. As a result, preventable control issues continue to occur. Which action would MOST improve stakeholder value?
c: Increase the frequency of assurance engagements.
Encourage earlier engagement through advisory services where appropriate.
Reduce communication to preserve independence.
Escalate the issue directly to the board.
e: Appropriate advisory involvement earlier in major changes can improve governance and prevent recurring control issues without internal audit assuming management responsibility, which is a more targeted fix than simply adding more assurance engagements, pulling back communication, or escalating straight to the board.

q: A newly appointed CEO asks the CAE to guarantee that fraud will always be detected through internal audits. What is the BEST response?
c: Agree, because fraud detection is internal audit's primary responsibility.
Explain that internal audit provides reasonable, not absolute, assurance.
Recommend eliminating management's fraud monitoring activities.
Limit future audits to fraud-related engagements.
e: Internal audit provides reasonable assurance and cannot guarantee that all fraud will be detected, so the CAE should clarify this expectation rather than agreeing to an unattainable guarantee, suggesting management drop its own fraud monitoring, or narrowing the entire audit plan to fraud alone.

q: Management accepted a high residual risk after implementing a less expensive control than originally proposed. The risk remains within management's documented tolerance but exceeds the tolerance previously communicated by the board. What should the CAE do?
c: Accept management's decision because risk ownership belongs to management.
Report the situation to the board using the established escalation process.
Recommend that management immediately implement the original control.
Reclassify the engagement as a consulting engagement.
e: When a residual risk exceeds the tolerance previously communicated by the board, the matter should be escalated through the established process, even though management believes it falls within its own documented tolerance, rather than simply deferring to management, dictating a specific control fix, or reclassifying the engagement type.

q: A CAE is updating the annual audit plan. Two engagements have identical risk ratings. One supports a major strategic initiative beginning next month, while the other involves a mature process with no recent changes. Which engagement should receive higher priority?
c: The mature process because historical data are more reliable.
The strategic initiative because of its greater uncertainty.
Both should receive equal priority.
The engagement requiring fewer audit hours.
e: Significant organizational change generally increases risk and audit priority, so the engagement supporting the new strategic initiative warrants higher priority than a stable, unchanged process, even with identical risk ratings on paper.

q: An audit of privileged user access identifies one administrator account that bypasses multi-factor authentication. Management explains it is needed for emergency system recovery and has never been abused. What is the BEST audit conclusion?
c: The control is effective because no incidents occurred.
The exception should be evaluated within the overall control framework before concluding.
The account should be removed immediately.
No finding is necessary because compensating controls always eliminate risk.
e: Internal audit evaluates whether overall controls adequately manage the associated risk, so the exception needs to be assessed within the broader control framework rather than being excused by a clean incident history, resolved by immediate removal, or dismissed on the assumption that compensating controls always fully offset risk.

q: Near the end of fieldwork, management provides additional evidence that changes one audit finding from "High" to "Moderate" risk. What should the engagement team do?
c: Note the evidence in the workpapers but keep the original risk rating since testing has already concluded.
Revise the conclusion if the evidence is reliable and sufficient.
Downgrade the finding to a minor observation without formally reevaluating the risk rating.
Ask the audit committee to determine the rating.
e: Conclusions should reflect all relevant, reliable evidence obtained before reporting, so late-arriving evidence should be evaluated and, if reliable and sufficient, used to formally revise the rating. Documenting the evidence without updating the rating, or softening the finding's status without a formal reassessment, both leave the conclusion out of step with the evidence, and rating a finding is the engagement team's responsibility rather than the audit committee's.

q: During an engagement, internal audit observes that the board receives extensive financial reporting but very limited information regarding cybersecurity, third-party risk, and business continuity. Which concern is MOST significant?
c: Financial reporting receives too much attention.
The board may lack sufficient information for effective oversight.
Internal audit should begin auditing only nonfinancial risks.
Management should stop preparing financial reports.
e: Effective governance requires information covering the organization's significant risks, so the core concern is that the board may not have enough visibility into cybersecurity, third-party, and continuity risks to exercise effective oversight, not that financial reporting itself is excessive or should be cut back.

q: The CAE can either outsource a specialized cybersecurity audit or postpone three moderate-risk operational audits due to staffing limitations. Which factor should MOST influence the decision?
c: Auditor preference.
Relative impact on achievement of the audit plan and organizational risks.
The number of reports that will be issued.
Historical completion rates.
e: Resource decisions should focus on addressing the organization's most significant risks, so the CAE should weigh the relative impact each option has on the audit plan and overall risk coverage rather than staff preference, report counts, or past completion statistics.

q: An auditor identifies a statistically significant deviation rate during testing. Management argues the deviation has no practical effect because no losses have occurred. What should the auditor evaluate NEXT?
c: Whether the deviation affects control effectiveness and audit objectives.
Whether management agrees with the sampling results.
Whether additional losses occurred after fieldwork.
Whether similar findings existed five years ago.
e: Audit conclusions depend on the effect of deviations on control effectiveness and the engagement objectives, not solely on whether a loss has actually materialized, so the auditor should assess that impact rather than deferring to management's agreement, waiting for future losses, or looking at historical findings.

q: Which indicator BEST demonstrates that the internal audit activity is aligned with organizational strategy?
c: Average audit report completion time.
Percentage of audit coverage devoted to strategic and emerging risks.
Number of recommendations issued.
Average engagement budget.
e: Strategic alignment is best demonstrated by the percentage of audit coverage devoted to the organization's highest-priority strategic and emerging risks, rather than by activity metrics like report turnaround time, recommendation counts, or budget size.

q: Senior management believes internal audit should avoid informal discussions during engagements to preserve objectivity. The CAE believes ongoing communication improves engagement quality. Which approach is BEST?
c: Avoid communication until the final report.
Maintain appropriate communication throughout the engagement while preserving objectivity.
Communicate only with the audit committee.
Allow management to determine communication frequency.
e: Timely communication throughout an engagement improves understanding and quality without compromising objectivity, so the best approach maintains appropriate ongoing dialogue rather than withholding all communication until the final report, restricting it to the audit committee, or letting management set the pace.

q: Following a significant control failure, the board asks why internal audit did not identify the issue during the previous audit. The engagement had been scoped to exclude the failed process based on the approved risk assessment at that time. What is the BEST response?
c: Accept responsibility because every significant issue should be detected.
Explain how the approved risk assessment determined the engagement scope.
State that management is solely responsible for controls.
Recommend repeating every prior engagement.
e: The CAE should explain that the engagement scope was determined using the approved risk assessment and the information available at the time, since internal audit provides reasonable assurance based on that scoping rather than guaranteeing every issue will be caught, and shifting blame entirely to management or proposing to redo every past engagement wouldn't address the board's question.
